summary: Defines the security architecture for WebRTC, the protocol suite for real-time applications deployed in browsers.

plainLanguage.summary: The plan for how browser video calls are kept private and checked.

questions: what is the webrtc security architecture
what is the sdp identity attribute
what is an idp proxy in webrtc
subtitle: How a browser keeps WebRTC calls private and verified, even when the calling website is not fully trusted.

tldr.problem: A WebRTC call is set up by a web server's JavaScript, so the browser must stop a hostile or compromised site from bugging the user, attacking others, or listening in.
tldr.mechanism: The browser acts as the trust anchor: it asks for device permission per HTTPS origin, verifies consent with ICE before sending media, encrypts with DTLS-SRTP keys the page cannot read, and can bind a peer's identity to the call key through an identity provider.
tldr.outcome: The call can be protected even against the signaling service, but the identity provider mechanism in Section 7 has not been widely adopted or implemented.

facts.label: Data channel security
facts.value: All data channels MUST be secured via DTLS

today: RFC 8827 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the architecture companion to RFC 8826; the RFC itself says its IdP-based peer authentication has not been widely adopted or implemented.

sections.title: The Trust Model
sections.content:
The architecture assumes a hierarchy of trust rooted in the browser, which serves as the user's Trusted Computing Base. Any security property the user wants must ultimately be guaranteed by the browser, or by something the browser verifies. If the browser is compromised, no guarantees are possible.

Other parties fall into two groups. Authenticated entities are calling services (web sites whose origin can be verified, ideally via HTTPS) and other users (peers whose identity can be verified cryptographically, ideally via DTLS-SRTP). Being authenticated does not make them trusted, but it lets the user decide whether to trust them. Everything else is unauthenticated and must be assumed to behave maliciously, so the system has to be secure even then.
sections.plainLanguage: The browser is the one grown-up you can count on. It checks who everyone is, and anyone it cannot check gets treated like a stranger.

sections.title: Anatomy of a Secure Call
sections.content:
The overview follows a best-case call between Alice and Bob who both use a calling service and each have an identity provider (IdP). Alice clicks Call, and the page creates a PeerConnection object, which needs no security check. Adding camera and microphone tracks is the first check: the browser asks Alice for permission. The signaling message then carries media information, ICE candidates and a fingerprint attribute binding the call to a key pair, plus an identity assertion obtained from her IdP that binds her identity to that fingerprint.

Bob's browser verifies the assertion directly with Alice's IdP, so the check is not mediated by either signaling server, and shows trusted information in the browser chrome. Bob's reply carries the same kinds of data. Alice and Bob then run ICE checks to verify media consent, and a DTLS handshake on every component ICE established. The exported keys protect SRTP for media and SCTP over DTLS for data channels. If both used IdPs, they also know the signaling service is not mounting a man-in-the-middle attack. Finally, WebRTC implementations must send periodic keepalives using the consent freshness mechanism in RFC 7675; if one fails and no new ICE channel can be established, the session ends.

The call still works if either side has no IdP; they just get a lower level of assurance. An anonymous call simply omits the assertion.
sections.plainLanguage: Alice and Bob each show an ID card from someone both can check. Then their computers swap secret keys, and the website passing notes between them cannot read the notes.

sections.title: The SDP Identity Attribute
sections.content:
A new session-level SDP attribute, identity, lets an endpoint convey its identity assertion to its peer. Its value is base64, and the decoded value is a JSON object with two keys: assertion, an opaque string consumed by the IdP, and idp, a dictionary naming the IdP. The assertion is bound to the endpoint's DTLS-SRTP fingerprints, and the attribute MUST cover all fingerprint attributes in the session description. Implementations SHOULD include only one identity attribute.

The offerer includes it in the offer, and the answerer may include or omit it independently. A receiver that fails to verify an identity MUST discard the offer or answer as malformed. When a session is modified with an unchanged set of fingerprints, the sender may reuse the same attribute; if the fingerprints change, it must send a new attribute or none, and the receiver discards all previously established identities.
sections.plainLanguage: The identity attribute is a name tag stuck onto the call request. It is tied to the call's key, so nobody can move the tag to a different call.

sections.title: Permissions, Consent and Media Security Rules
sections.content:
This section turns the threats from RFC 8826 into requirements. The basic unit of permission is the origin, and the origin is only secure over HTTPS, so clients MUST treat HTTP and HTTPS origins as different permission domains and refuse all permission grants for HTTP origins. WebRTC is disabled on mixed-content pages, and if a page becomes mixed content mid-call the implementation MUST end the call or show a warning.

Camera and microphone access needs explicit consent, supporting at least one-time and permanent grants. The UI MUST show when devices are in use in a way scripts cannot suppress. Permanent screen sharing permissions cannot be granted from a script request, and screen sharing needs its own dialog. For consent to receive traffic, browsers MUST implement ICE, verify reachability before sending any non-ICE packet, and MUST NOT expose the ICE transaction ID to JavaScript.

For IP privacy the API must let a script suppress ICE until the call is answered, and restrict candidates to TURN. For media security, implementations MUST support SRTP, DTLS and DTLS-SRTP, must not send plain RTP or negotiate NULL ciphers, and MUST NOT offer SDP security descriptions. All implementations MUST support DTLS 1.2 with TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and the P-256 curve. The API must generate a new key pair for every call by default, use different keys per origin, and never let JavaScript read negotiated keying material. Clients also need an inspector UI showing the security characteristics of the media.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the browser's house rules: ask before turning on the camera, show a light while it is on, check the other side wants the data, and keep the encryption keys where the website cannot touch them.

sections.title: Web-Based Peer Authentication
sections.content:
Sometimes the browser should identify the far end without trusting the signaling service, for example on a minimally trusted poker site when calling someone known from a social network. The RFC adopts the usual three roles: the Authenticating Party (AP) trying to prove who it is, the Identity Provider (IdP) vouching for it, and the Relying Party (RP) verifying. Here the AP and RP are the user and their browser, not the signaling site. IdPs are either authoritative (they control that part of the name space, like an email domain) or third-party (they attest without controlling it, so the RP must trust them explicitly and their number must stay small).

The browser's PeerConnection loads JavaScript from the IdP into an isolated "IdP proxy" and calls a generic API to create and verify assertions, so the browser needs no built-in knowledge of any identity protocol. The proxy page lives at a well-known URI of the form /.well-known/idp-proxy/ plus the protocol, over HTTPS. An assertion is a JSON object with the idp and assertion values. Verification returns an identity in the form user@domain and the original contents. The browser must check that the DTLS certificate in use matches the fingerprints in the assertion, and reject an identity whose domain differs from the IdP's unless the IdP is a trusted third party under local policy.

The RFC itself notes that the working group was too optimistic about enthusiasm for this mechanism, and that at the time of publication it had not been widely adopted or implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: An ID check by a trusted office. The browser asks that office, not the website, to confirm who the caller is, and it ties the answer to the call's key.

sections.title: Residual Threats and Failure Cases
sections.content:
The security section covers what is left over. Without HTTPS to the signaling server or the identity mechanism, any on-path attacker can swap the DTLS-SRTP fingerprints and impersonate an endpoint. Even with HTTPS, the signaling server can attempt a man-in-the-middle unless keys are checked independently; a malicious service can strip identity assertions but cannot forge new ones. Content JavaScript MUST NOT be able to use DTLS keys, even to sign, or it could authenticate a call under a key it controls.

For privacy, protections assume a non-malicious calling service, and they cost performance through TURN relays and delayed ICE. For denial of service, consent protects victims that do not run WebRTC, but WebRTC endpoints such as a call center can be flooded through data channels, which need no user consent. The RFC describes attacks where the signaling service swaps ICE candidates or cross-connects offers and answers, and defenses such as flow control, ignoring misbehaving calls and responding to ICE Binding Requests for only a limited number of remote ufrags.

The IdP mechanism depends on the proxy checking it runs in the IdP's origin, on the well-known URI, and on care with confusable characters in identities. Third-party cookie blocking can break IdPs that use cookies for login.
sections.plainLanguage: No lock is perfect. This part lists what could still go wrong, like a dishonest website passing notes or someone flooding a phone line, and what the browser does to limit the harm.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The document registers the identity SDP attribute, a session-level attribute with Mux Category NORMAL that carries an identity assertion binding an identity to the transport-level security session. It also registers the idp-proxy well-known URI suffix, with the IETF as change controller.
sections.plainLanguage: It adds two new entries to official lists, one for the name tag and one for the web address where the identity page lives.
